details: Yakiniku Like wants to help diners get some likes of their own . Japan has a lot of yakiniku restaurants, where you grill your own meat, but Yakiniku Like is different from the rest. Whereas typical yakinuku places have their grills set into table for a group of dining companions to gather around, all of Yakiniku Like’s seats are at counters, with an individual-size grill for every customer . This setup, complete with your own personal selection of sauces and controls for the strength of your grill’s fire, makes Yakiniku Like the perfect place for solo diners who’re craving yakiniku, But just because you happen to be eating alone doesn’t mean you’re not a socially minded person, and so one of Yakiniku Like’s branches in downtown Tokyo has created a special seat specifically for customers who want to take photos and record videos of themselves to share on social media . Situated in a corner of Yakiniku Like’s Shinjuku Minamiguchi branch , just a short walk from bustling Shinjuku Station, Studio Like , as the special seat is called is equipped with handy self-photography equipment such as a lighted vanity mirror for checking hairstyling and makeup, camera mounts for overhead filming, and a backdrop and surrounding walls to guarantee some extra personal space and for the benefit of other customers who’d rather not be featured in someone else’s pics or video clips. title: Beloved, 100-year-old Tokyo public bathhouse Sengenyu is about to get a second life this December
summary: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. details: Various entities take a dip together to save a community institution and preserve public bath culture for the next generation to enjoy. Public bathhouses , known as sento in Japanese, have long served as important community gathering hubs where different generations can interact with one another. Unfortunately, not all public baths are able to stay afloat in this age of rising costs and other factors. Case in point: from 2015 to 2025, the number of public bathhouses operating in Tokyo dropped from 628 to 417 locations. Thankfully, one public bath in Tokyo’s Nerima Ward called Sengenyu is not going to join those statistics anytime soon. First opened in 1927, the third-generation previous owner was on the verge of closing the beloved community staple due to their family’s increasing age and the deteriorating facilities. However, thanks to the Tokyo Public Bathhouse Succession Matching Program offered jointly by the Tokyo Metropolitan Government and the Tokyo Public Bathhouses Association, a new owner in company Ofuro Works was found. Now, instead of being demolished, Sengenyu is currently being renovated and will reopen to the public in early December. ▼ The current exterior of Sengenyu The project includes large-scale remodeling of Sengenyu’s entrance, lobby, changing rooms, and saunas to update certain facilities. ▼ Rendition of the completed exterior, designed to blend in with the surrounding area The lobby is particular is intended to become a spacious, relaxing entryway where patrons can soak in the warmth of the natural wood theme inside. In addition, a new electric heater from Japanese bath company Metos will be installed within the saunas. Patrons can continue to throw water on the rocks themselves in order to increase the steam to their desired level. These new updates don’t mean that Sengenyu will lose all of its original charm, though, as features such as the retro-style bathroom with its colorful tile art and the Shigaraki ware tanuki statue outside will be preserved in its redesign. In a delightful community collaboration, Ofuro Works is also partnering with students at the local Nihon University College of Art to design an updated logo and mascot character based on the tanuki statue. It’s a true full-circle moment, as students from this school as well as other local universities have long been going to Sengenyu and can now leave their own personal mark on the space for many more years to come. Finally, widespread public fundraising efforts are set to begin on November 1 through Japan’s largest crowdfunding site, Campfire . The project aims to raise 1 million yen (US$6,375) to help offset the costs of remodeling and updating the bath facilities. Financial backers will receive a towel, t-shirt, and a sneak-peek of Sengenyu behind the scenes before it reopens for business. ▼ The art students’ new logo combines the steam of a bathhouse with the puff of smoke that occurs when a tanuki transforms in Japanese folklore. Despite the decrease in the total number of Tokyo public bathhouses, we can only hope that the statistics showing that the number of users is actually going up will allow Sengenyu and other bath facilities in the Greater Tokyo Area to flourish for 100 more years and beyond. title: Fishing information website for Susaki, Japan, hit by data leak, all 3 users affected
summary: Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised. For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times […]
details: Personal information for everyone posting to the site over the past year compromised . For the past week, there has been an inordinate number of hacking and data leakage from all kinds of websites, from 6.6 million people’s names, emails, and, in some cases, driver’s license info taken from major car rental and parking service Times to the details of registered users on the Burger King app. With new leaks being reported literally every day, it’s getting to the point where you’d be in the minority to not have been affected somehow. The latest data breach reported has come out of the city of Susaki in Kochi Prefecture . This coastal city with a population of about 20,000 people recently had their municipal fishing information website Tsuri-Baka City Susaki (Fishing-Crazy City Susaki) hacked. It appears that a company in Tokyo that manages the website’s servers was attacked and notified the fishing site on 16 October, causing them to shut down the site while an investigation is carried out. ▼ The entire Fishing-Crazy City Susaki website is down as of this writing. As a result, everyone who used the site’s inquiry form from July 2025 to July 2026 may have had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, and details of their fishing inquiry compromised. According to the fishing bureau’s records, as many as three people may have been affected during this period. The details of the inquiries have not surfaced on the dark web but could range anywhere from how they’re bitin’ on a specific day to recommendations for a good restaurant that’ll clean and cook the day’s catch. The current downtime is also a concern, with as many as one person potentially unable to request fishing information for the area from an official government source as opposed to other reviews on the Internet or just talking to people around town. Online comments expressed a difficulty in facing the full severity of this hack, with some resorting to humor as a defense mechanism. “Wouldn’t it be easier just to apologize to those three people directly? Why tell all us?” “Maybe all the victims can go on a fishing trip together.” “This data breach is on a completely different level from anything we’ve seen before.” “Honestly, it takes guts to come forward and admit this. I respect that.” “I guess that’s a good thing, for some people at least.” “It’s kind of scary that even places like that are getting hit.” “I would like to apply for the job of the person handling their inquiries.” I think the positive spin that can be put on all this is that it’s quite likely only a few people used the inquiry form of Fishing-Crazy City Susaki because it is such a comprehensive website and rich in detail that almost no one reading it would be left with any questions to ask. And by providing such stellar information, they managed to keep the fallout from this server attack to an absolute minimum. It just goes to show that in these times of increasingly tenuous cyber-security, our first line of defense is quality fishing information. title: Is this crazy-looking home sauna just what our busy daddy reporter needs in his life?
summary: Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home. Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. Now, though, he’s got a wife and kid, plus an apartment out in the suburbs that’s closer […]
details: Ahiruneko’s single-guy sauna days are done, but this gadget promises to bring the steam right into his home . Back in his bachelor days, our Japanese-language reporter Ahiruneko used to go to a sauna once or twice a week. Now, though, he’s got a wife and kid , plus an apartment out in the suburbs that’s closer to the mountains than the office , and thus a long commute, leaving him with only enough time for one or two sauna days in an entire year. So in his quest for the optimal sauna/life balance, he decided to purchase a home sauna . Converting an entire room of his home into a sauna facility would be excessive in terms of cost and floorspace, so instead of doing that he went looking for a home sauna kit on Rakuten, where he found an assemble-it-yourself steam sauna kit for 17,780 yen (US$112). All of the components shipped together in a large cardboard box, and Ahiruneko laid them out to see what he’d be working with. Folded up inside that cloth pouch is the material for the sides of the sauna tent, pictured with it in the above photo are a floor mat, piping for the tent’s frame, one device for producing steam, another for dispersing it inside the tent, and a hose to connect them . Also included in the set were a folding chair and one of those rollers that are supposed to stimulate the pressure points on the bottom of your feet to provide various vague wellness benefits. The included instructions were written in less-than-fluent Japanese, but between them and the photos on the Rakuten product page here , Ahiruneko could figure out what he needed to do. He started by removing the tent material from its pouch and assembling the pipe frame . This was a pretty quick and simple process, and before long the tent was standing in the middle of his living room. It almost looks like a giant down vest, with a slot for your neck and also two little slits that you can open if you want to reach your hands outside the tent . There’s also an exterior pocket where you can keep the remote control to turn the steam generator on and off or adjust the temperature. Speaking of the steam generator, it resembles a rice cooker . You fill it with water, and once the liquid gets hot enough to start turning into steam, it gets channeled through the side of the tent by the connecting tube… …and dispersed by the steam box, which you place inside the sauna with yourself. The dimensions of the tent are cozy, but there’s room to spare in which to fit the chair, and laying down the mat before your steam session will help keep your floor from getting damp. OK, with everything assembled, it was time to turn ono the steam generator! Ahiruneko hit the power button…and had no idea what the display said. That blurriness isn’t from Ahiruneko’s camera. His brand-new home sauna’s display was foggy and indistinct, almost like it was censoring itself with a mosaic. Luckily, the control buttons all had legible labels, and the printed instructions had told Ahiruneko that once steam started coming out of the top of the sauna tent, it was ready for him to step in . It took about 20 minutes for the steam to heat up , but when it did, entering the tent turned out to be surprisingly tricky, since the frame has a pair of connected pipes running horizontally across the front. Ahiruneko ended up having to temporarily pull them apart, step inside the tent, and then put them back together. Now that he was finally inside, all he needed to do was zip the front back up… … and settle in for a steam session . If you’re setting one of these up for yourself, you’ll definitely want to give your housemates a heads up beforehand, so that they don’t wander into the room and think you’ve been decapitated, or maybe had your body from the neck down converted into machinery in order to become a sauna cyborg. But as startling as this setup looks when viewed from the outside, it was extremely relaxing for Ahiruneko on the inside . He’d purposely kept his expectations low about how high the temperature could get, but it turned out that the steam filling his home sauna was surprisingly hot. It wasn’t long until his body was sweating steadily, but his head being exposed kept the environment from feeling stifling or even stuffy. In time, though, Ahiruneko started to sweat from his face too, so he unzipped one of the arm holes so he could grab the remote control and turn down the temperature just a bit. He’d actually put a second remote control in the pocket too, the one for his TV, since having his own personal sauna means he can watch whatever he wants while staming. As for negatives, the device that emits steam inside the tent does, understandably, get very hot, so you do need to be conscious of where it’s placed and make sure not to step on it. You also need to wipe down the tent and let it dry before you fold it back up, which adds a little time and hassle to the start-to-finish process. Still, even with some cleaning up to do, Ahiruneko is still coming out ahead, time-wise, by being able to have a sauna session without having to leave his home. He thinks he’ll still probably look for opportunities to treat himself to a trip to a professional sauna when he has the chance, but for those times when his schedule or budget is tight, he’ll be very happy to use this at-home version again. details: Who wowed our reporters the most with sheer friendliness? Our website has been around for quite a while now, and over the years we’ve even had the opportunity to rub shoulders with famous movie stars and musicians from time to time. Considering we’re known for behavior that some may deem “ gross ” or “ indecent ,” it wouldn’t be too shocking if they treated us like the schlubs we admittedly are, but there have been a few who really seemed to shine as genuinely good people. So, our Japanese language writers would now like to take a moment and give credit where credit’s due to the famous people from Japan, as well as famous people from abroad who visited Japan, who really made a positive impact on us . When it comes to celebrity interviews, P.K. Sanjun is usually our frontline reporter. As such, he’s met the likes of Will Smith , Arnold Schwarzenegger , and Tom Holland , to name a few. But here are the people who made the biggest impression on him. ● Chris Pratt I’ve interviewed a lot of Hollywood actors, and they’ve all been really nice. I sort of think you need to be in order to make it out there. But among them, Chris Pratt stood out as a super nice person. When I finished my interview, I was just sitting there feeling awkward, but he took the initiative and said, “Hey! Let’s take a photo together!” It was a god-tier gesture and made me fall in love with the guy. View this post on Instagram ● Maximum the Ryo-kun He’s a very private person. You could even say he’s mysterious, and very artistic too. But he’s also an absolute legend and totally down to earth when you talk to him. So much so that I found myself wondering, “Does a celebrity like this actually exist?” The rest of the band [that he’s in, Maximum the Hormone], were great too. Nao-chan immediately snapped a picture after Ryo-kun shaved my eyebrows. Even though it’d been years since I last interviewed them, Daisuke-kun greeted me with a friendly “Long time no see!” Of course, Ue-chan, who shyly chatted with me about kendama , was wonderful too. In short, Maximum the Hormone aren’t just great because of their music. They’re a class act as well. If I ever get another chance to meet Ryo-kun, I want to ask him why he loves [’80s Japanese rock band] Lindberg so much. View this post on Instagram Mr. Sato ’s been known to do a few interviews in his days as well, including none other than Santa Claus . But what big names managed to out-nice even Ol’ Saint Nick for our star reporter? ● Cunning Takeyama I’ve met the famous Japanese comedian Cunning Takeyama a few times now, and every time his genuine kindness shines through. His work often involves interacting with the general public in TV segments, so he seems to make a conscious effort to make people feel at ease. That gentle, approachable character he shows the moment he meets someone is something that I aspire to emulate as an adult. View this post on Instagram ● Shinichiro Azumi I’ve been invited on his TBS radio show Nichiyo Tengoku a few times. Even though it’s a live broadcast, he went out of his way to look after me because of my lack of experience in this setting. He has a way of completely managing the flow of conversation but never lets it show by drawing stories out of me naturally. It’s the mark of a true professional and made a strong impression on me in the way I could relax and have a natural conversation with him. You don’t often see Yoshio interviewing famous people, unless it involves a money-making scheme , but he’s often behind the camera at these meet-ups and has interacted with plenty of famous people as well. Here’s who made the biggest impact on him. ● Matt Damon I was a photographer at an interview with him during the release of Jason Bourne. He might be a world-famous actor, but he didn’t act like it at all and answered every question from P.K. with sincerity. I’ve been present for a lot of celebrity interviews, but Matt Damon was the nicest of them all. It really took me aback how humble someone of his stature could be. He was just a very cool guy. ● Yumi Adachi I was the photographer when Seiji interviewed her while pretending to be Yngwie Malmsteen . I always thought she had a very elegant fashion sense and way of life, so I was intimidated to meet her, but she turned out to be incredibly friendly and cheerful, exactly like she is on television. While we were standing around waiting, she noticed I had the latest iPhone at the time and said, ‘Wow, it’s got three lenses!” I still have and cherish that phone to this day. ▼ Yumi Adachi and Yngwie Malmsteen (Seiji Nakazawa) The interviews where Seiji Nakazawa pretended to be Yngwie Malmsteen in an effort to join famous people’s musical projects were always dicey ones. They rarely ended up being actual interviews, and the famous people involved would have had every right to chew us out for making a mockery of the whole process. But it’s also a chance for celebrities to really show how easy-going they can be, as Ahironeko recalls. ● Non This was our very first Yngwie project , and I was the photographer. The awkward tension in the air was so thick both for us and the people on her side. None of us really knew what was going on. Considering that, it wouldn’t have been a surprise if she just snapped at us with, “Excuse me… What the hell are you doing?” But she was all smiles the whole time. A true goddess. View this post on Instagram Takashi Furusawa is a newer addition to our staff and hasn’t been to as many interviews as the others. But that doesn’t mean he hasn’t had his own brushes with greatness. ● Miki Narahashi Miki Narahashi is best known as the voice of Misae Nohara in the long-running hit Crayon Shinchan . But for me, she was also my senpai when I was at voice acting school. I still clearly remember how she always looked out for me, giving me advice and kind encouragement when I had problems. It was a true honor to have studied under her for two years, and I still cherish that experience to this day. ▼ Narar

title: This Tokyo snack shop can send your taste buds on a trip around Japan for just 1,000 yen
summary: There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo. In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would […]
details: There’s a new sweets curator in downtown Tokyo . In an ideal world, we’d spend every single day on a meandering journey through Japan, stopping see the sights and sample the delicacies whenever and wherever the mood struck us. Unfortunately, we don’t have the copious amounts of money or free time that such a lifestyle would require, but there is a way to send your taste buds on a trip across Japan for a very affordable price, as we found out on a recent visit to the Marui Annex department store in downtown Tokyo’s Shinjuku neighborhood. On the first floor of the building you’ll find a shop named Edited Japan Shinjuku , which just opened in September . “Edited” isn’t being used with the meaning of revising or altering something, though, but more in the sense of an “editor’s selection,” as Edited Japan is a curator of Japanese regional sweet and salty snacks. The store is stocked with over 100 different items, representing all of Japan’s prefectures , and unlike some food souvenir shops that only offer large-quantity boxes, Edited Japan specializes in individual-serving sizes, letting you pick out a variety of treats without making any major commitment as you search for a new favorite. Another cool thing about Edited Japan is the store’s focus on snacks that are a genuine part of everyday life in their local communities . You won’t find anything that’ll win you brownie points with a snooty coworker or snobby classmate here. Instead, the shelves are filled with things that present a combination of high quality and reasonable price. Think more “This is something people in Kyoto would munch on if they want something sweet on a Sunday afternoon” than “Bring this to the next party you’re invited to so you can show off your refined sensibilities.” So we decided to see how many prefectures’ treats we could taste with a budget of 1,000 yen (US$6.30), and we mean a hard limit of 1,000 – not a single yen more. Thankfully, this still gave us plenty of room to work with, since most of Edited Japan’s items are somewhere in the 100-200 yen range . We had to do some mid-shopping calculations to make sure we didn’t go over, but in the end, we were able to put together a bundle of snacks from six different prefectures, with the total coming to 995 yen . So what did we get? Let’s start at the north of the country, and work our way down, which makes our first entry on the list Hokkaido Dining Kitchen’s Corn Soup (130 yen), from Hokkaido Prefecture . Soup may not be counted as a “snack” in some cultures, but certain varieties in Japan do sort of get treated that way. Corn pottage, for example, is commonly seen as something that’s tasty and moderately filling even when it’s not served as part of a meal, which is why you’ll often see cans of corn soup for sale in Japanese vending machines during the fall and winter. This powdered corn pottage mix, though, is tastier than what you can get from a can, as it’s made with an especially sweet variety of Hokkaido-grown corn and contains no artificial flavors or preservatives . Next have Dutch Senbei rice crackers, from Yamagata Prefecture’s Sakata Beika , which were the value all-star of our shopping trip, priced at just 45 yen. This brand of rice cracker has been a big hit in Yamagata since 1962, but what makes them “Dutch,” other than the cap that person is wearing in wrapper illustration? There are two theories, one of which is that the distinct bumpy texture of the crackers is said to resemble the footprints left by visitors from Japan to the Netherlands, some of the first foreigners to set foot on Japanese soil back in the feudal era, and thus some of the first people to be seen walking around in Western footwear, which was much bulkier than the straw sandals that were the norm for Japanese people at the time. The other possible explanation is that Oranda , the Japanese word for both Holland and Dutch, sounds similar to orada , a way of saying “we” in the Yamagata dialect, which would make “Oranda Senbei” (as the snack is called in Japanese) sound similar to saying something like “the rice crackers we made.” Regardless of why they’re called that, though, Sakata Beika’s Dutch Senbei are crisp and refreshing, lightly salted to enhance, but not replace, the natural flavors of the non-glutinous Yamagata-grown rice that they’re made with. Next we move on to Kyoto , which means it’s time for nama yatsuhashi . Nama yatsuhashi is a folded triangle of soft mochi with a dollop of anko (sweet red bean paste) inside. Chewy and sweet, with just a touch of sophistication from a dusting of cinnamon , nama yatsuhashi are so popular with Kyoto residents and visitors that there are a few different companies that make them. Nishio , who makes the 250-yen matcha -flavored version we picked up, is one of the most respected, because if your company has been around since 1689, you’ve earned a lot of trust. Since nama yatsuhashi’s simple ingredient list lends itself well to experimentation, most makers, Nishio included, have a cycle of seasonal flavors that are only offered at certain times of year, but the matcha ones are so well loved that they’re available pretty much all the time, as long as the day’s stock isn’t sold out. Continuing west, our taste buds arrive in Hyogo Prefecture , where the coastal town of Akashi brings in some of the country’s most delicious octopus, inspiring rice cracker maker Eirakudo to make Akashi Takosen senbei (250 yen). These deep-fried senbei are made with Akashi octopus and treated with a savory, slightly sweet sauce , and they’re just as suited for a midday snack as they are for a pairing with a nice cold beer after work. We shift back into sweets mode as we reach Hiroshima Prefecture , which, like Kyoto, has a particular dessert that’s overwhelmingly associated with it: the momiji manju . Hiroshima Prefecture is famous for its beautiful maples, called momiji in Japanese, and these manju (sweet dumplings) are shaped like the trees’ leaves. The outside

title: Mochido donuts make a squishy return to Lawson stores across Japan

details: Mochido or Mochidon’t. There is no Mochitri . Earlier this year, we stumbled upon a pair of donuts sold by convenience store chain Lawson that completely redefined the genre of convenience store donuts. They were called Mochibee ( Mo-chee-bay ), and came in powdered sugar and roasted soybean (kinako) flavors. Though they tasted delectably sweet, the whole experience was a bittersweet one because this was just a limited trial run, and Mochibee weren’t sold nationwide. But our writer Natsuno Futon was delighted to hear that Lawson have finally gotten their act together and re-released these treats all over Japan, starting on 20 October. However, the name has changed to Mochido , perhaps because the “beh” part of the name led people to think they were bagels instead of the similarly shaped donuts. Hoping only the name was different, she hurried to her nearest Lawson on the evening of the 20th, only to find they were already sold out. Unsure if they were really that popular already or if her timing was just unlucky, she decided to give up for the night but was able to find them the next morning. The same flavors of sugar and kinako were there, and Futon picked up one of each. The price was just the same as before: 171 yen (US$1.10) each. At a glance, they looked exactly the same as she remembered them, with their slightly irregular shape a testament to their chewy fluffiness and a gracious coating of sweet powders. Futon decided to start with the plain sugar , and after cutting off a piece, it seemed to have that same layered texture as before. She reminisced about that delightfully crisp surface, enhanced with cracker flour and poppy seeds. Unable to hold out any longer, she popped a piece into her mouth and was immediately transported back to that blissful afternoon snack last March. It was every bit as good as it was back then, possibly even better somehow. Next, she tried out the kinako flavor . Obviously, the texture was just as good here, but what really knocked it out of the park for this one was the perfect balance of kinako that made its presence known but didn’t overpower the innate deliciousness of the donut itself. Both donuts had incredible attention to detail and seemed more like the kind you’d buy from a bakery rather than a convenience store. Futon was overjoyed after thinking she’d lost these treats forever after the last time. However, she also crunched the numbers, and the calorie intake from these two decadent donuts far outweighed the calories burned during her 30-minute walk to and from the store. This imbalance would not bode well for her waistline, but thus is the life of a donut lover . Photos ©SoraNews24 ● Want to hear about SoraNews24’s latest articles as soon as they’re published? details: Chainsaw-wielding robots prove they can contribute to human mobility in ways other than people running away from them in terror . Japan’s rail network is famous for its sterling safety and reliability records, and neither of those would be achievable without a whole lot of preventive maintenance. East Japan Railway Company (a.k.a. JR East ), one of the nation’s largest rail operators, is constantly monitoring the condition of its tracks and carriages in order to spot potential problems before they occur, and when it spots an issue that needs to be addressed, it dispatches a crew to take care of it. And sometimes some of the members of those crews are chainsaw-wielding robots . JR East’s maintenance division had noticed that tree branches growing over the tracks near Nobeyama Station in Nagano Prefecture needed to be cut and cleared away, in order to keep them out of the way of trains traveling on this section of the Koumi line. To do so, they rolled out one of their new multifunction heavy railway machines, a humanoid robot attached to a vehicle capable of traveling on rails like a train or on streets like a truck . The robot’s left hand is a multi-pronged claw, suited for grabbing and moving branches and other debris, but where things get really awesome is the right hand, which is a chainsaw. The robots appear to be updated versions of the units JR West started using in 2024 . JR East began adding the robots seen in the above videos to its maintenance fleet in March of this year, but there have only been limited opportunities for the public to see them. The company has traditionally tried to schedule its maintenance projects for the middle of the night, so that they can be completed in the time between the last train of the night and the first of the morning, so as not to disrupt service for passengers. An increasing number of maintenance workers have been requesting day shifts, though, and the company is looking to accommodate them, which also affects the robots’ usage, since the machines are human-operated. Online reactions to the JR East robot’s day at Nobeyama have included: “All of a sudden, we’ve got the kind of awesome robots I’ve always dreamed about.” “Yes! It’s so cool how the left and right arms are different.” “Total R-O-B-O-T vibes.” “It reminds me of the robot from [Studio Ghibli’s] Laputa.” “Is this the robot that the T-800 Terminator is gonna get developed from?” “So should we call this a ‘labor,’ like they call the mecha in the Patlabor anime?” “Hey, didn’t I see that thing in Contra: Hard Corps’ train stage?” “It’s a robot, but it’s also kind of cute.” JR East says that shifting a greater number of maintenance projects to daylight hours will necessitate more frequent closures of line during their regular operating hours, but hopes that passengers will be understanding, and acceptance will most likely be easier to accept if they come with the promise of more chances to see robots in action. title: 93-year-old Japanese grannie helps set trap for scam artist half her age
summary: This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it. details: This woman was the target of a criminal scheme, but she definitely wasn’t going the be the victim of it . Over the past few weeks, Japan has seen a sharp spike in the number of data leaks and cyberattacks, with many organizations warning citizens that their personal information may have been compromised. So on October 21, when a 93-year-old woman living in the town of Aisho, Shiga Prefecture , received a phone call from a man informing her that he was a police officer, and that there had been an unauthorized withdrawal of funds from her back account, it was cause for concern. He did assure her, though, that because the problem had been detected quickly, they could remedy it in a swift manner too. The police would need her help to do so, though. First, he instructed her to freeze her bank account. Second, he said that the authorities would need to examine her ATM card, but to make that part of the process as convenient as possible for her, he said that he could send an investigator to pick the card up at her home . Finalizing that pickup time took a little extra conversation, with the woman talking to the man on the phone the next day as well, but eventually they agreed that the investigator would come that very day, October 22, to take come get the card. Now, there are a number of warning lights that might be going off in your head right now. For starters, if there’s been some kind of anomaly with your bank account, it’s usually your bank that will contact you, not the police. Your bank will probably want to be part of the conversation too if you need to relinquish possession of your ATM card, and it’s also sort of unusual for the police to do house calls to pick up evidence rather than asking you to come down to the station. So it’s pretty clear that the woman was the target of scammers . Unfortunately, this sort of scheme, taking advantage of senior citizens’ trusting nature and confusion regarding technology and bureaucracy, is a time-tested, reliable way of defrauding them, and the 47-year-old man who came to pick up the her ATM card was probably feeling smugly satisfied from proving his superior intellect compared to the befuddled woman. However, the woman turned out to be far savvier than the fraudster had bargained for. She hadn’t been sitting in her living room wringing her hands between phone calls. She’d sniffed out that this was a scam, so she got in touch with the nearby Higashiomi Precinct of the Shiga Prefectural Police . She then pretended to have been fooled , but when the man pretending to be a police officer came to her house, there was a squad of real police officers already there, lying in wait, and instead of getting the woman’s ATM card, the man got arrested . As he hasn’t entered a plea or gone to trial, yet, currently his arrest is for “suspicion of attempted fraud.” Honestly, though, of you show up at the door of an elderly woman who’s never met you before and tell her she needs to give you her ATM card, the only possible explanation other than fraud would be if you were robbing her, so things aren’t looking good for him from a legal standpoint either way. It’s unclear whether the man who came to the woman’s home is the same man who’d called her on the phone, but police (the real police) believe that he was working with other criminals to set up the scam, so hopefully they’ll be apprehended as well, perhaps with the help of an equally large network of tough-as-nails grannies. title: Japan’s mission to Martian moon and back underway
summary: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing. At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this […]
details: This mission is expected to be the first-ever Martian moon landing . At 4:41 a.m. on 20 October, an H3 rocket took off from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture. It was carrying the MMX (Martian Moons eXploration), one of Japan’s largest-ever spacecraft, with a weight of 4,480 kilograms (9,877 pounds), and as of this writing, all systems are operating normally. ▼ And was there ever any doubt that there’s also a cute mascot version of MMX? The MMX’s mission is to travel to Phobos, one of Mars’ moons, land there, pick up samples, and bring them back to Earth. It’s one of the most ambitious Mars missions to date, but Japan’s space agency JAXA has already made a name for itself by landing on asteroids and returning samples successfully on two previous endeavors. Considering Phobos is up to ten times the size of those asteroids and locked into Mars’ orbit, this might seem like an easier mission. However, the key factor is overcoming the gravity of both Phobos and Mars. The MMX will have to make a soft landing on Phobos, then take off again in order to return to Earth. As a result, about 68 percent of the spacecraft’s total weight is just propellant. It is hoped that by collecting material on Phobos, we can learn more about how it and Mars’ other moon, Deimos, were formed. The two leading theories are that they were once asteroids that got captured by Mars’ gravity or that they formed from the debris expelled by a massive collision of something with the red planet. In addition, it is said that about 0.1 percent of material on Phobos is actually Martian soil , having been ejected when meteorites struck the planet. The goal of the MMX is to pick up at least 10 grams of material from Phobos for an estimated 0.01 grams of actual Martian material. ▼ Here’s a simulation of how it should all go down in a nutshell. Whether this will be the first sample from Mars transported by humans back to Earth remains to be seen, however. China is currently preparing to send its Tianwen-3 to Mars, where it will collect 500 grams of pure Martian soil and bring it back to Earth. Both projects are scheduled to return here in 2031, so if everything goes as planned for everyone, it’ll be a relative photo-finish to see which country will be the first to break off a piece of Mars and carry it back. Going according to plan is a big “if” as well. The MMX was originally expected to launch in 2024, but development of the H3 was delayed and the very tight window when Earth and Mars are properly aligned once every two years closed. China will also need to make sure everything progresses like clockwork from now until their launch in 2028 to avoid their own two-year delay. Regardless of whoever does get back first, these samples will help to blow open our understanding of the Martian environment, including the possibility that life once or even still exists there in some form. Then, maybe we can finally get back to checking out our neglected other neighbor Venus someday. It’d be pretty funny if all this time there actually were a bunch of aliens living in those boiling sulphuric clouds, wondering why no one ever comes looking for them. title: Middle Eastern juice bar B-Fresh lands in Harajuku

details: Refresh yourself with fruity sweetness while the crowds have yet to discover the store. Japan’s cafe culture is a flourishing landscape of specialty roasters, themed cafes , and retro junkisssa coffeehouses . However, the presence of large foreign players, led by companies like Starbucks and Gong Cha, can’t be understated due to their expanding presence in the sector. Recently, a budget, large-capacity coffee brand from South Korea, Fave Coffee, has been opening locations one after another, while the world’s largest food and beverage chain Mixue from China is also steadily increasing its number of stores. In this environment, B-Fresh , billing itself as “a brand from the Middle East ,” has made its first splash into the waters of the Japanese market with opening a store in Tokyo’s Harajuku neighborhood on October 1 . Our ace reporter Mr. Sato was slightly worried it would already be bearing the brunt of the throngs of young people that flow through Harajuku’s streets, he still decided to give it a go. About three weeks after the opening of the store, Mr. Sato stepped foot into Harajuku, and despite it being a weekday, Takeshita Street was crowded as usual, with places like Marion Crepes seeing no drop in customers regardless of day or time, with people lining up endlessly. Scouring the streets, Mr. Sato was sure that he was in the right area and was keeping an eye out for one of these telltale lines, indicating a store’s popularity, but it turns out there was no line for B-Fresh at all. This meant great convenience for Mr. Sato, but he lamented the fact that it had just opened and felt kind of desolate already. It may just be that word of mouth for the store hasn’t spread yet, and business will pick up in the weeks to come. On top of that, it looked as if the building is undergoing exterior wall construction , so if there hadn’t been a sign indicating they were open as usual ( tsujodori eigyochu , 通常通り営業中), an uninformed passerby might assume they were not open at all. The store itself is a juice bar that serves smoothies using fresh fruit, acai bowls, and yogurt , with a variety of items that Mr. Sato was unfamiliar with or unsure how to choose. Using the ticket vending machine inside the store, Mr. Sato chose based on appearance and ordered something called B-Pink Brûlée , priced at 1,100 yen (US$7)] for a large (please note that only cashless payments are accepted in the store). While waiting for his order, Mr. Sato inspected the menu some more. The products seem to be broadly divided into three categories: bubble drinks, smoothies, and acai bowls and frozen yogurt . The main representative of the bubble drinks is the Bubble Tea, and you can also choose fruit juice-filled pearls. For smoothies, there are drinks that blend things like Nutella and Oreos along with fruit, and toppings such as superfoods like chia and flaxseed can be added to any order. The range of customization really is quite wide. In light of the numerous options and indecisiveness, Mr. Sato focused on which menu photos looked appealing, but seeing the actual drink itself, he was confident that his choice was not wrong as it looked incredibly delicious. ▼ Plenty of whipped cream and strawberry crunch on top Making up the drink was a mix of strawberries, vanilla milk, and “creme brulee ,” but even after drinking it, Mr. Sato wasn’t quite sure what the creme brulee was actually represented by—he believes it might be the custard cream. The menu photo also showed strawberry pearls inside of it, but that was an additional topping for 100 yen, so Mr. Sato passed on it this time. Even without the additional pops of fruit, it was deliciously sweet. Amid the unseasonably hot weather and a feeling of fatigue after his morning pole dancing practice, the flavor was very refreshing. In the end, it remains to be seen whether or not this brand can catch on in Japan, but for now, it appears that crowds are yet to form. details: Pikachu Sweets bakes up new treats to celebrate Pokémon’s 30th birthday . This year marks the 30th anniversary of Pokémon , which is another way of saying it’s the franchise’s 30th birthday…and everyone knows you can’t celebrate a birthday without cake, right? And if you’re looking for a cake to celebrate this particular birthday, there’s no more appropriate choice than a Pikachu cake . That’s exactly what’s coming to Tokyo’s Pikachu Sweets by Pokémon Cafe next month. Not to be confused with the full-scale, sit-down Pokémon Cafe near Tokyo Station , Pikachu Sweets is a dessert stand located inside the Sunshine City shopping/entertainment complex in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro neighborhood. Seen in these photos is the Poké-patissiers’ newest creation, the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich , made of two Pikachu-shaped slices of moist, fluffy shortcake with whipped cream and sliced strawberries between them , giving you a mix of sweet, tart, and milky flavors. Served in a little celebratory paper holder, this is a shortcake you can eat without your hands without getting your fingers messy , and the raised corners of the holder should keep the cake securely in place as you raise it up to snap a photo before your first bite, maybe with the Pikachu Sweets storefront in the background. Coming to the menu on the same day as the Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich is a new dessert drink, the Eevee Chocolate Frappe , with an adorable Eevee Pokémon 30th anniversary cookie and a swirl of whipped cream sitting atop the slushy chocolate drink , creating a color pattern evocative of Eevee’s coat. If you order a Pikachu Shortcake Sandwich plus an Eevee Chocolate Frappe or a Catch ‘Em Latte (“Get Latte” in Japanese) also gets you one of three 30th anniversary stickers with an illustration of a Pikachu wearing a cafe uniform. The lattes come in four different varieties (caffe latte, tea latte, caffe mocha, or caramel latte), hot or cold, and they’ll also be getting 30th anniversary foam art . The lineup goes on sale November 5 and will be available until December 31 , with both the Pikachu cake and Eevee frappe priced at 1,200 yen (US$7.60). Pikachu Sweets has no actual eat-in space, so customers generally either take their treats home or enjoy them on one of the benches within Sunshine City or in the adjacent outdoor plaza. title: Super Mario creator Shigeru Miyamoto to receive Order of Culture from Japanese emperor
summary: If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him. Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture. These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and […]
details: If anyone deserves an Order of Culture, it’s-a-him . Every year, the Japanese holiday of Culture Day is observed on 3 November. This is also the day that the Emperor of Japan bestows the Order of Culture on selected citizens who made significant contributions to Japanese culture . These include researchers, leaders of industry, artists, doctors, and more. And when it comes to people who made an impact on Japanese culture, I doubt there’s anyone who’d disagree that Shigeru Miyamoto belongs in that group. After creating one of the most influential games of its time, Donkey Kong , in 1983, he played a critical role in revitalizing the slumping global video game industry with Japan at its center through Super Mario Bros. in 1985, creating both a revolutionary style of game and iconic characters that would thrive for the next 40 years. And everything he’s done since then, such as contributions to classic franchises like Zelda , Mario Kart , Star Fox and Pikmin, is just a ton of thick, sweet icing on the cake. In honor of this, Miyamoto will be presented the award by Emperor Naruhito at the Imperial Palace alongside seven other recipients , including Kenso Soai, who also won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry this year, and Shunichi Tokura, the composer of Pink Lady’s smash hit “UFO” and the current chair of JASRAC . In a press conference following the announcement, Miyamoto said, “I am truly happy to have found video games. As a creator, I have just as much fun developing games as the players do playing them. It is a joy to be able to keep doing this.” He also had the following advice for younger game designers: “I often tell them it is better not to start with a game they’re already a big fan of and find entertaining and just try to tweak it to make it ‘more fun.’ Instead of refining something that already exists, it is much more rewarding to start at the core and ask yourself, ‘Wouldn’t it be interesting if I tried this?’ Then focus your energy on building something from that idea.” Miyamoto will also be the first person from the gaming industry to have received this honor. After the news broke, there was an outpouring of support and congratulations from people all over Japan in online comments. “It’s long overdue, but wonderful news. Mario and Zelda are beloved not just in Japan but all over the world.” “I make recipes but was happy to hear he feels the same joy in his work and always thinks ‘Wouldn’t this be interesting?’ like I do.” “Even as the game market has grown to a huge scale, Mario and Zelda continue to rank among the top-sellers. He is a person who shaped countless lives all over the world.” “His work influenced our youths, the way we spent time with our family, and some of our unforgettable memories.” “Miyamoto never pandered to trends and always asked himself if his creations made people feel something.” “When he started out, video games were seen negatively. Now, his characters have appeared at the Olympics !” “I remember being completely hooked on Donkey Kong. I tried the famous shortcut trick over and over but could never do it!” “Paul McCartney even asked for Miyamoto’s autograph when they met and greeted him by singing the Super Mario song.” Speaking of Paul McCartney, it’d probably be fair to say that the next person from the game industry who should get an Order of Culture is none other than Koji Kondo, whose scores for Super Mario Bros. and Zelda were just as impactful and enduring as the games themselves. title: Tokusatsu hero “Moonlight Mask’s” pocket change donations help traffic accidents victims in Japan
summary: Small change and a big heart. A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask, a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping […]
details: Small change and a big heart . A fun and really sweet aspect of Japanese culture is the trend of anonymous donations made in the name of masked people. Easily, the most iconic of these is Tiger Mask , a title taken by several people donating expensive randosel school bags to orphans and needy families and helping out in other ways. Based on a wrestling manga hero of the same name, these real-life heroes have also led to a variety of copycats and spin-offs. I think there was even a kind-hearted Jason Mask one time. And every New Year’s Eve since 1974, on Sado Island in Niigata Prefecture, police have discovered a bag full of coins at one of their stations and outposts, along with a note that reads, “These are coins I collected, one by one every day. I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little,” and is signed “Gekko Kamen,” meaning “Moonlight Mask” in English and also occasionally localized as “Moonbeam Man.” Hardcore tokusatsu fans will likely know one or more of these names as the precursor to the entire genre of superhero kids TV shows. Originally airing in the ’50s, Moonlight Mask was the archetypal masked, motorcycle-riding crusader of justice. Every year the police honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and donate the coins to funds supporting those orphaned by traffic accidents. However, very recently, something truly unexpected happened. On 19 October, in Niigata City on the mainland of the prefecture, a police officer approached his patrol car and found an envelope on the windshield. Inside were coins totaling 240 yen (US$1.53) , and on the envelope a note said, “I’d be happy if it can help those suffering due to traffic accidents, even if just a little.” On the same day, about 1.5 kilometers from the first incident, another envelope was found at a police box in the Shirone Chuo area of the city. This one contained 299 yen (US$1.99) in change and had a note with the very same legendary words of Moonlight Mask. In both cases, no witnesses spotted anyone leaving the envelopes. This would mark the first time in over 50 years that Moonlight Mask or someone else using the same moniker donated to victims of car accidents outside of Sado Island. ▼ News report showing the envelopes and coins Deputy Chief Ryo Takahashi of the Niigata Minami Police Precinct said they will honor Moonlight Mask’s wishes and forward the 539 yen to children orphaned by traffic accidents. He added, “I am deeply moved by this person’s unending concern for the victims of car accidents. Because they are a hero, we are not investigating to uncover their true identity.” We can probably all agree that a noble deed should be respected regardless of its magnitude. However, this particular magnitude wasn’t enough to cover a combo at McDonald’s, and some readers of the news online had trouble fully coming to terms with that. “Oh… Well…” “I thought the report just had a typo in the number.” “It is the thought that counts, I guess…” “It’s always been New Year’s Eve. So why now?” “He does donate often. I looked it up, and this is his 53rd donation. Last time he gave 30,010 yen.” “I guess the rising cost of living is even putting a strain on Moonlight Mask.” “I wonder if this person is extremely poor themself.” “I want to say the amount isn’t important, but at a certain point wouldn’t this be considered a form of harassment?” “Only a horrible person would laugh at a gesture like this.” “This person must be pretty old by now. That was probably a good amount of money in their day.” “Their handwriting is very neat. They must be very meticulous.” “539 was the license plate number of Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle! Do your homework before shooting off your mouths!!!” That last comment would have been a cool detail, but a fun fact is that Moonlight Mask’s motorcycle had the license plate number Mu-8323 or 8328. Though it can be hard to see with from the angles the TV series’ scenes were filmed at, and with 1950s-quality cameras, some eagle-eyed fans were able to catch a peek of the superhero’s road-legal bike and at least narrow it down to those two. It’s especially ironic because while within the series private detective Juro Iwai is heavily implied to be Moonlight Mask’s secret identity, this is never confirmed, and even the actor for Moonlight Mask is listed as “?” in the credits. But anyone even remotely inclined to find out who he is need only look at the back of his bike and run a check on it. It just goes to show that the true spirit of Moonlight Mask is to help those in need and right the wrongs of society at all costs, even if your plan isn’t all that well thought out. title: Ghibli composer Joe Hisaishi named Composer-in-Residence of Los Angeles Philharmonic
summary: Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences. details: Multiyear relationship will include new works specially created for L.A. audiences . At the age of 75 and with a career that’s already spanned more than 50 years, it wouldn’t be unnatural for Joe Hisaishi to be easing into retirement. Or maybe it would be, since the acclaimed composer best known for creating the soundtracks to Studio Ghibli’s most beloved anime films, including My Neighbor Totoro , Princess Mononoke , and Spirited Away , since Hisaishi continues to display a boundless passion and enthusiasm for making music and sharing it with as wide an audience as possible. For example, en route to setting a couple of Guinness World Records , he held a series of concerts at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles over three days this past July. If you missed your chance to see him then, don’t worry, because Hisaishi has now been named Composer-in-Residence of the Los Angeles Philharmonic orchestra . This isn’t some simple honorary title/goodwill ambassador deal either. The L.A. Phil is describing the relationship as “a five-year creative partnership” that will start with the upcoming 2027/2028 concert season . In addition to recurring performances at all three of the organization’s customary venues (the iconic hillside Hollywood Bowl, the adjacent John Anson Ford Amphitheatre, and the downtown Walt Disney Concert Hall), Hisaishi “ will create new works specifically for the LA Phil and its audiences ” while also engaging in new commissions, recording projects, and educational and community outreach endeavors. “Los Angeles holds a special place in my musical life-from the premiere of my Harp Concerto with the LA Phil’s Emmanuel Ceysson at Walt Disney Concert Hall to our recent performances at the Hollywood Bowl and The Ford,” said Hisaishi following the announcement, and also that he’s “deeply honored” to be chosen for the role. “In the seasons ahead, I look forward to exploring new musical horizons with this extraordinary orchestra and sharing the spirit of discovery with audiences in Los Angeles and beyond.” ▼ An audio clip of one of Hisaishi’s previous Hollywood Bowl concerts View this post on Instagram ▼ With Hisaishi scheduled to be spending a lot more time in L.A., he’ll also be able to check out America’s first One Piece store , should the mood strike him. Hisaishi’s resume isn’t composed entirely of Ghibli soundtracks, as he’s also made contributed selected compositions or arrangements to other anime including Mobile Suit Gundam , Children of the Sea , Kimagure Orange Road , and Creamy Mami , as well as creating the soundtrack for video game Ni no Kuni and a handful of live-action Beat Takeshi movies. There’s no denying, though, that Hisaishi is most strongly associated with the work he’s done for Ghibli, As a matter of fact, there’s never been a Hayao Miyazaki-directed Ghibli feature film that Hisaishi didn’t write the score for, and with the studio’s track record of leaving a deep impression on fans around the world with its soundscapes, no doubt the new creative journey Hisaishi is about to embark on will be another movingly memorable one. Recently, our ace reporter Mr. Sato told us that he needed to go to Toranomon Hills , a shopping and entertainment complex in downtown Tokyo’s Toranomon neighborhood . Why? To eat ice cream. As Mr. Sato explained, recently he’s been seeing photo after photo of the soft serve ice cream from Dolce Tacubo , a dessert cafe located in Toranomon Hills, that’s been going viral. “Once the algorithm decides ‘You like this kind of stuff, don’t you?’ and starts filling your social feeds with it, you end up wanting to try it more and more, right?” he told us while heading out the door. Honestly, we’ve never known Mr. Sato to need any prodding by outside forces to convince him to eat ice cream, but we trust his savvy sense when it comes to photogenic sweets, and we anxiously awaited his report…which almost didn’t come in. Like a lot of Japanese shopping centers, Toranomon Hills has a food section, called T-Market , in its basement area. Mr. Sato assumed that’s where he’d find Dolce Tacubo, but after making multiple laps of the place, he still couldn’t find the cafe . So next he took the elevator up to the higher levels of the building, but he still couldn’t find it. Even consulting Google Maps didn’t clear things up, since the app told him to exit the building entirely, then come back in through another entrance, which didn’t make any logical sense to him. Eventually, it was human intelligence that put him on the right path, as Mr. Sato asked the Toranomon Hills employee posted at the taxi stand where he could find Dolce Tacubo, and they informed him that the cafe really is the T-Market zone, on basement level 2 , so back down the escalator our reporter went. At the risk of offending the sensibilities of interior designers with a penchant for minimalism, T-Market’s aesthetics might be a little too elegant for their own good. A number of the understated storefronts don’t have the shop’s name prominently displayed above their entrances, which is how Mr. Sato managed to walk right past this place multiple times … … before he finally realized this actually is Dolce Tacubo! He’d been almost ready to give up and go home before he spotted the surprisingly unassuming sign for Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve, but now that he knew he was in the right place, it was time to try the viral-hit dessert for himself. The ice cream is available in three varieties, vanilla, kabocha/Japanese pumpkin, and “mixed,” which gives you both flavors together. The vanilla is 1,000 yen (US$6.30) and the kabocha 1,200, which are premium prices for ice cream in Japan, and it’s a little weird that the mixed cone is 1,300 yen, more expensive than an all-kabocha cone despite half of it being the less-expensive vanilla ice cream. But hey, desserts aren’t always logical, so Mr. Sato decided to splurge on a mixed cone, and waited in the café’s eat-in space while the staff prepared his treat. It was every bit as beautiful as he’d hoped it would be . Amazingly, the swirly ridges of vanilla and kabocha wound through and wrapped around each other without any smearing save for a small section at the very top. The roasted pumpkin seeds are a classy touch too, and there’s so much care put into the presentation that it almost feels like personal pampering, putting a big smile on Mr. Sato’s face. Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is more than just a proverbial pretty face, too . Both of the types of ice cream are rich and flavorful. If you’ve never had kabocha sweets before, they tend to be both lighter and sweeter than what you’d get with Western-style pumpkin pie, and this is an outstanding example of how well it can work as an ice cream flavor. In terms of texture Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is actually on the firmer end of the spectrum within the category, dense enough that you can easily stand a spoon in it when it’s just-served. It melts easily on the palate, though, and has a silky mouthfeel without any significant grittiness. Mr. Sato can’t finish his taste-testing notes without mentioning the waffle cone too . It’s got a nice, substantial weight to it and a stimulating crunchiness that makes for some great synergy with the smooth ice cream. Beautiful, delicious, and interesting, Dolce Tacubo’s soft serve is a high-quality dessert by any metric, and Mr. Sato feels it definitely justifies not only its cost, but also the determination it might take to find it. title: One simple unexpected recipe swap will make your Japanese-style omelets extra fluffy and juicy
summary: And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still. In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet, you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). […]
details: And one more cooking hack will make your dashimaki tamago fluffier still . In terms of ingredients, dashimaki tamago is an incredibly simple dish. A type of Japanese omelet , you can make it with just three ingredients: eggs, water, and dashi (a stock made from fish and kelp that’s found in all sorts of Japanese dishes). The cooking process is also pretty straightforward, or maybe paradoxically straightforward, since dashimaki tamago is basically an omelet that you wrap ( maku ) back over itself multiple times, using a rectangular frying pan if you want the traditional squared-off shape. But just because dashimaki tamago is simple doesn’t mean it’s easy to make. The process can be surprisingly delicate, and while anyone with minimal cooking skills will be able to make dashimaki tamago that’s edible, it takes a deft hand to make dashimaki tamago with a wonderfully fluffy texture throughout its layers . So when we heard rumors of an unexpected ingredient substitution that’s supposed to make dashimaki tamago extra fluffy, we were all attentive ears and growling stomachs. First, let’s run through the basics of how to make dashimaki tamago . You’ll need: ● 3 eggs ● 1 tablespoon of dashi (we used the type called shirodashi) ● 3 tablespoons of water Mix them all up in a bowl, and also heat up an oiled frying pan on medium heat. Pour 1/3 of the mixture into the pan, give it a little mix with cooking chopsticks, and once it’s half-cooked, roll it to the front half of the pan. Reoil the now vacant part of the pan, add half of the ingredient mixture, and repeat the cooking and rolling process, then do it all again for the remainder of the mixture. So what’s the cooking hack substitution we’re trying today? Using sparkling/carbonated water instead of regular water . We heard about this idea through Asahi TV’s news/talk program Tantei! Knight Scoop , and then our reporter Natsuki Gojo headed into the SoraKitchen to test it out. Aside from the water swap, there’s only one other change to make, which is that when using the sparkling water, you mix the egg and dashi together first, and then add in the sparkling water right before cooking . OK, let’s see if this sparkling water swap really is such a bright idea! ▼ Regular water (left) and sparkling water (right) Starting with how the mixture of the three ingredients looked prior to cooking, as you can see in the above photo there’s a noticeable amount of fizz introduced by the sparkling water…at least initially . After stirring, though, the bubbles died down, and the regular and sparkling mixtures were equally calm. Once Natsuki poured them into the pan, though, the bubbles came back to the sparkling mix in a big way . Once both dashimaki tamago were done cooking, we laid them out side by side on a plate, and sure enough, the sparkling version had cooked up bigger and plumper, despite both versions having the exact same volume of ingredients . Next we sliced off a piece from each to examine their cross-sections, and were happy to see that the sparkling water substitution had produced exactly the sort of results we’d been hoping for! The regular-water version had congealed towards the bottom of the roll, but the sparkling dashimaki tamago had maintained a nice network of little air pockets while cooking, and those had made it fluffier. It wasn’t just the texture that had been enhanced, either. The sparkling dashimaki tamago was juicier too . Emboldened by this success, Natsuki decided to whip up one more batch of dashimaki tamago to test out another rumor she’d heard for further fluffiness . This time, instead of using three tablespoons of sparkling water, she used 175 milliliters (5.9 ounces), or roughly 10 tablespoons. Unsurprisingly, this resulted in even more bubbles at the pre-mix and cooking stages, and Natsuki found herself worried that the mixture might be too watery to cook up properly. But those fears turned out to be unnecessary, and this high-volume sparkling water version was the fluffiest and juiciest of all three she cooked . ▼ Sparkling water dashimaki tamago (left) and high-volume sparkling water dashimaki tamago (right) Natsuki herself is quick to point out that she doesn’t have a ton of experience cooking her own dashimaki tamago, so we’re not saying that using sparkling water is a must for good results. At the same time, her relative inexperience proves that you don’t have to be an expert to benefit from this simple ingredient swap, so if you’re looking to make your Japanese-style omelets as fluffy as you can, this is definitely worth giving a shot. title: This curry restaurant might have the worst location in Tokyo…or maybe the best
summary: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of […]
details: Alk Road finds a way to turn a negative into a positive . There are a lot of curry restaurants to choose from in Tokyo , but Spice Curry Alk Road stands out from many of its rice-and-roux rivals by virtue of its outstanding customer reviews. Diners are so satisfied that they’ve made Alk Road one of the top 100 curry restaurants in Tokyo based on average review scores on Tabelog, Japan’s most popular user-submitted restaurant site. Alk Road is just a one-minute walk from Iidabashi Station , so you could say that it has a great location…but as we found out on our visit, you could also make an argument that it has the worst location for a curry restaurant in Tokyo. If you head to the restaurant’s address, you’ll find yourself in front of this building. And yes, you will see the word “curry,” written in Japanese as カレー, on the signage . But the writing in front of “curry,” 上等? They’re the characters for “Joto,” as in “Joto Curry,” a curry restaurant chain that is not the independent Alk Road . So if you were to amble up here, you might think that Alk Road has gone out of business and been replaced by a Joto branch. A restaurant closing down and then a different one with the same specialty moving into the same spot isn’t all that unusual in Japan, since it lowers the renovation costs that you might have with, say, converting a yakiniku restaurant into a conveyor belt sushi joint. However, if you look down at the entrance to Joto Curry, you’ll see that Alk Road’s name is written next to the door … … and both Joto Curry’s and Alk Road’s names are written on the noren (cloth banner) hung above the entrance . Things get even more confusing when you step inside, since the first floor is clearly a Joto Curry branch. If you want to find Alk Road, what you have to do is turn to your right… …and follow the arrows pointing you up the stairs to the second floor… …and then, finally, you’ll have arrived at Alk Road! View this post on Instagram Yes, Alk Road has the confusing misfortune of being a curry restaurant that you can only access by first passing part-way through a different curry restaurant, and one that’s part of a famous chain to boot . This might seem like a recipe for constant animosity between the upstairs/downstairs neighbors, but it turns out that Joto Curry and Alk Road aren’t exactly direct competitors . Whereas Joto’s specialty is Japanese-style curry, Alk Road’s focus is on Indian-style curry, which the second-floor restaurant’s chef makes from scratch every day. While they’re both variations on the same basic concept (curry and rice), they use different kinds of roux, and different kinds of rice too – long-grain Indian rice for Alkroad’s curry, and short-grain Japanese rice for Joto Curry’s. So among diners in Japan, these two restaurants’ offerings are scratching different culinary itches, and even if you are in a perfectly 50-50 mood as to which type of curry they were craving, Alk Road actually offers a way to enjoy both in the same meal . One of Alk Road’s menu items is the Special Combination , a plate of curry rice in which one half is Joto’s roux and a pork cutlet, and the other is your choice of one of Alk Road’s house-specialty spice curries. ▼ Our 1,400-yen (US$8.80) Special Combination of Johto katsu curry and Alk Road chicken spice curry You also choose between Indian and Japanese rice for the Special Combination. We asked for the Indian rice, which made for a unique mixture of flavors and textures when paired with the Japanese roux. Both curries were excellent on their own, with Alk Road’s giving us a complex mixture of spices and seasonings and Joto’s being a more straightforward spiciness with a hint of sweetness in its flavor profile, and at the center of the plate where it flowed into one another we got yet another intriguingly fresh flavor. Should you want even more variety, Alk Road’s counter has an array of spices that you can shake onto your curry at your discretion, such as Cayenne pepper, roasted cumin, garam masala, and ajwain chili powder. This one-of-a-kind collaborative curry combination is something that’s only possible by nature of having two different curry restaurants operating so close to one another, and through it Alk Road has cleverly turned a negative aspect of its location into a positive. So while the search for Alk Road might be a little confusing, it’s well worth going to the trouble to find, just like with a certain soft serve ice cream specialist elsewhere in Tokyo . title: Baum vending machine in a Yokohama station lets us eat cake served on a luxury cruise ship
summary: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. details: Our favorite kind wasn’t even the one we expected, but they were all the baum-dot-com. It takes a lot to surprise us when it comes to Japanese vending machines , considering we’ve seen everything from Sriracha to sushi meals being sold in them. While the latter might sound a bit dubious, we’ve had relatively good results with the weird and wacky, and we’re always keeping our eyes peeled for new discoveries. The latest unusual vending machine we spotted was right outside of the ticket gates at Bashamichi Station on Yokohama’s Minatomirai Line . It was actually attracting a lot of curious glances from passersby, most likely because it was filled with Baumkuchen , the German spit cake that’s incredibly popular in Japan and usually goes by just “baum.” ▼ Cake from a vending machine somehow feels a lot safer than sushi. A closer look at the sign revealed that this particular baum was produced by Cocotomo Farm , which makes a 100-percent gluten-free cake using homemade rice flour from Aichi Prefecture. According to the sign, its brown rice-based hard baum is even given as a welcome gift on the luxury Asuka III cruise ship –Japan’s largest passenger ship–and was being sold in this machine at a discounted price to reduce food waste. Apparently there’s an Asuka III Meets 47 Prefectures Project , and this brand was selected as a representative for the Aichi Prefecture Room. As for why it’s being sold at this particular nondescript station in Yokohama, well, that part’s still a mystery–but perhaps it’s because there are several international cruise ship terminals in the area. There were plenty of baum options in the vending machine, but none of the selections were for the brown rice-based hard baum variety alone. Therefore, we opted for a combo pack with a slice of that one along with a slice of the white rice-based soft baum for 650 yen (US$4.14) , as well as a pack of hard baum edges for 500 yen. ▼ The machine takes cash or a variety of payment apps. All of the baum in this machine are frozen to preserve their freshness, so our prizes were quite chilly when they first came out. Luckily, the weather was relatively warm on this particular day, and the slices of cake had thawed out well by the time we got home. Here they were in their simple, unpretentious packaging. We were journalistically obligated to then immediately sample the slices of the soft and hard varieties, which were individually packaged. ▼ Soft baum (top) and hard baum (bottom) The soft baum was true to its name and had a refined, moist texture. We would have never known that it was gluten-free if the packaging didn’t alert us. Meanwhile, the hard baum had the exact opposite kind of feel. It was densely packed and required some force to bite down on, being chewy at the same time. It also carried the distinctive almost nut-like flavor of brown rice. We had always assumed that all baum tasted more or less the same, but this sampling threw that notion far out the window. Next, we broke out the hard baum edges. There were six individual pieces of slightly varying sizes packed into one bag. The hard baum edges were, if anything, even more densely packed with flavor and texture than the soft baum and regular hard baum alike. Sure, they were rough-looking on the outside, but they hid an intense surprise on the inside. In fact, they ended up being our favorite of the whole bunch. The value of six pieces for that price was also hard to beat. We have no idea how long the Cocotomo Farm vending machine is going to be stationed at Bashamichi Station–but we suppose that whenever it goes away, we’ll just have to get our baum fix from the ample varieties sold at at Muji instead . title: Visiting the “world’s most precarious temple” in China, where getting there is half the battle
summary: Xuankong Si is surprisingly both extremely out of the way and extremely crowded.
